title: Error handling and defensive design
subtitle: Sort errors into the ones you expect and the bugs, handle each kind on purpose, and never hide one.

c.v: On 12 June 2025, many Google Cloud APIs started to return errors around the world. The cause was one part of Service Control, the system that checks
and policy for incoming API requests.
On 29 May, Google had added a new quota check to Service Control. It rolled out region by region, but the code path that failed never ran. It needed a certain policy change to trigger it.
The report says this change had no proper error handling, and it was not protected by a

On 12 June, a policy change was copied to every region within seconds. The policy data had blank fields that nobody intended. The new code read a blank field and hit a null pointer. The report says that "without the appropriate error handling, the null pointer caused the binary to crash."
The binaries restarted, read the same data and crashed again: a
. In big regions, the restarting tasks all hit the database table they depend on at once. Service Control did not have randomized
to prevent this. Full recovery in us-central1 took up to about 2 hours 40 minutes.
Google's fixes include better error handling and testing for invalid data. They also say parts of Service Control should "
Errors come in two kinds, and you should handle them differently.
happen in normal life. A user types a wrong date. A file is missing. Another service is busy for a moment. Your code should plan for these and handle them.
are broken assumptions. A value that "can never be empty" is empty. An index is past the end of a list. Retrying will not fix a bug. A person has to fix the code.
Rust's official book uses the same split. It calls them recoverable and unrecoverable errors. It says unrecoverable errors "are always symptoms of bugs."
Decide on purpose what happens for every error. Handle the expected ones close to where you can do something useful. Make bugs loud, so a person sees them and fixes them. Never hide either kind.
block, or a "log and return null" with no plan, hides the problem. The program carries on in a bad state, and the real failure shows up later, far away, where it is much harder to debug.
Step through a request where one downstream call fails. Watch how each layer decides what to do. Use Next and Back, or the ← and → keys.

Check data where it enters your system, before any business logic uses it. Check the shape (type and format) and the meaning, for example "the end date is after the start date". Define what you accept and reject everything else.
Do this on the server, even if the browser already checks the same field. OWASP also says to validate data from internal APIs, partner feeds, queues and stored records when it crosses a
The Google Cloud policy data came from inside Google, and it still had blank fields.

Some languages throw exceptions. Others, like Rust and Go, return an error as a normal value. Rust's book gives a simple rule that works in any language. When failure is expected, return an error value, so the caller must decide what to do. Its examples are a parser given bad data and an HTTP call that hits a
. When a contract is broken, stopping is reasonable, because it shows a bug in the caller.
The style matters less than one habit: every error must be visible in the code that calls the function.

means you stop at the first sign of trouble with a clear error. Do this for bugs, bad config at startup, and requests that are too large. Google's SRE book advises that under overload you should "fail early and cheaply."
means you still serve the user, with less. A product page can show without recommendations. The SRE book says degraded mode "shouldn't trigger very often", and that you should test it.
The choice depends on the feature. A missing recommendation is fine. A missing fraud check on a payment is not.
Retries, timeouts, circuit breakers and fallbacks
, the ones that may pass in a moment. Do not retry client errors or malformed requests, because the same request will fail again.
covers keys, backoff and retry limits.
Put a timeout on every remote call. Amazon's advice is to set a timeout on any remote call, and in general on calls between processes on the same machine too.
down the call chain, so lower services stop work the user has already given up on.

A circuit breaker stops calls to a service that keeps failing, for a short time. This protects the failing service and saves your threads. Amazon notes a cost: breakers add modal behavior that is hard to test, and they can slow recovery.

A fallback is a second way to get the answer, used only when the first way fails. Amazon usually avoids them. Fallback code is hard to test and may rarely run in production, so it can hide bugs. In an Amazon outage around 2001, web servers fell back to a database when their
failed. They all hit the database at once, and the whole website went down.
Amazon prefers to make the main path more reliable, or to run both paths all the time, which turns the fallback into
. If a fallback is essential, Amazon exercises it as often as possible in production.
Messages for users, logs for engineers

Users and engineers need different things. The user needs a short, calm message and a next step: "We could not load delivery dates. Please try again." Engineers need the details: error type, which call failed, how many attempts, and a request ID.
, SQL errors or server versions to users. They help attackers learn your system. Return a generic response and log the details on the server.

They get most of the page.

Only when you run and test it often.
for each call that can fail, write down which errors are expected and what happens for each. Everything else is a bug, and a bug should fail loudly.

sections.title: At work: how a senior uses this

c.v: In code review, ask about every
"What does the caller see, and what do we log?"
"What happens if this field is empty?"
for data from files, configs and other teams, not only from users.
Check that every remote call has a timeout, and that retries happen in one layer only.
Mark each dependency as critical or optional. Optional ones get a degraded mode. Critical ones fail with a clear error.
Make sure a degraded mode shows up on a dashboard, so it does not stay on for weeks unseen.
Keep one error format across all your APIs, with a code and a request ID in every response.
"List every place in this module where an error is caught and ignored, logged without being returned, or turned into null. For each one, say what the caller will see."
"For each remote call in this service, list the timeout, the retry policy and what happens on failure. Mark calls with no timeout."
"Write tests that send empty, missing and oversized fields to this parser. Each test must expect a clear validation error, not a crash."
The agent did not add broad
blocks that hide errors to make tests pass.
Retries are only on transient errors and only on idempotent calls.
Error responses do not contain stack traces, SQL, tokens or personal data.
New fallback code has a test that makes the main path fail.
Validation is on the server, at the boundary, not only in the client.

q.v: Your service calls a pricing API and gets HTTP 400 Bad Request. What should it do?

options.v: Do not retry. The same request will fail again, so return or log the error.
Switch to a fallback pricing service.

why.v: A client error means the request itself is wrong. Sending it again cannot fix it.

q.v: A function reads a config value that, by design, must always be there. It is missing. What is the best choice?

options.v: Use a default value and carry on quietly.
Treat it as a bug. Fail fast with a clear error that names the missing value.
Catch the error and return an empty result.

why.v: A broken assumption is a bug. Hiding it lets bad state spread and makes it harder to find.

q.v: What should the API send back to a user when a database query fails?

options.v: The full stack trace, so the user can report it.
The SQL query and the database version.
A short, generic message with an error code and a request ID. Details go to the server log.

why.v: Detailed errors help attackers. Keep details in your logs, where engineers can find them by request ID.

q.v: Why does Amazon's Builders' Library warn against fallback code?

options.v: It runs rarely, so it is hard to test and may fail or overload something when you finally need it.
It is always slower than the main path.
Cloud providers do not allow it.

why.v: Code that rarely runs can hide bugs. Amazon prefers to make the main path more reliable.
